1. The animation shows how inflation can erode a fixed income check. It uses US consumer prices (CPI-U) and is labeled illustrative, US-only, and "history, not a forecast." Each bar appears to be a starting month from 1947 to about 1986. A line marks the "first check" level.

2. Frames 1 to 4 highlight an early window of starting months, Sep 1947 to Jan 1949. Those bars are at or above the first-check line, and the highlight box is then zoomed in on. In frames 5 and 6 the view widens to run through Aug 2006. A "none since" band appears across the top, and a person named Ruth is marked at the right edge. The bars for later starting months sit lower, mostly well below the line.

3. My reading is that the bars show how far prices had risen, or how far buying power had fallen, relative to that first check. Starting in Sep 1947 to Jan 1949 was the high point. The "none since" label suggests that no later starting month got back to that level. The image doesn't define the bar height or the Ruth marker, so this is an interpretation. The most likely meaning is that a check that stays the same buys less over time.

4. A viewer, and I'm picturing a 64-year-old weighing two annuity payout options, might take away that a flat payout loses buying power over a long retirement. They might then lean toward an option with inflation adjustment, or at least think about it. That is a cautious inference, not a firm instruction.

5. The animation didn't state this advice. It only showed the history and said it was "not a forecast." The advice is my own conclusion, based on the context of choosing between annuity options.
